theory.intro: **Parallel box plots** are two box plots drawn on the same scaled axis, so two datasets can be compared at a glance.
facts: Both box plots must share the **same scale**, so the two datasets can be compared directly.
A **narrower box** means a smaller IQR: the middle half of the data is more tightly clustered and more consistent.
The **median** divides ordered data into halves: estimate about half above and half below. Repeated values can affect exact counts.
steps: Read the minimum, lower quartile, median, upper quartile and maximum on the common scale.
Compare the medians to see which dataset is generally higher or lower; use the context to decide whether higher or lower is better.
Compare the range (maximum $-$ minimum) and IQR (upper quartile $-$ lower quartile). A smaller IQR means the middle half is more consistent.
For a threshold question, locate the threshold relative to the median or quartiles and estimate the proportion. Repeated values can affect exact counts.

workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) Medians: $A=46$, $B=52$. Class B has the higher median because $52>46$.
(b) Class A: range $=88-13=75$, IQR $=63-29=34$.
Class B: range $=81-19=62$, IQR $=59-38=21$.
Class B has the smaller IQR, so its middle half is more consistent. It also has the smaller range.
(c) Class A has the higher maximum, $88>81$. The maximum is the best single mark; the median describes the middle of the marks. They need not give the same comparison.

(a) Both medians are $44$ and both maximums are $91$.
(b) Class C: range $=91-11=80$. Class D: range $=91-4=87$. Class D has the larger range.
(c) Class C: IQR $=61-26=35$. Class D: IQR $=54-33=21$.
Class D has the smaller IQR, so its middle half is more consistent, even though its full range is larger.

(a) Crew A has the lower median: $31<36$ minutes, so it generally finishes faster.
(b) $33$ minutes is below Crew B’s median of $36$ minutes. Using the box plot, estimate less than half the times were below $33$ minutes.
(c) $36$ minutes is the median, so the estimate is about $50\%$. Repeated times can affect the exact numbers above or below a threshold.

Team R’s maximum is $43$, so none of its scores exceed $43$.
Team S’s minimum is $43$, so none of its scores are below $43$.
Their scores just touch at $43$. Every Team S score is at least as high as every Team R score; a shared boundary does not mean identical datasets.

workedExamples.question_text: Two datasets have the same maximum, $97$. Dataset E has range $63$ and Dataset F has range $46$. Which has the lower minimum, and what is it?
workedExamples.solution_text:
Range $=$ maximum $-$ minimum, so minimum $=$ maximum $-$ range.
Dataset E: minimum $=97-63=34$.
Dataset F: minimum $=97-46=51$.
Dataset E has the lower minimum, $34$.

mastery.question_text:
A golf club records scores for the same $40$ players on two courses.
Both courses share the same maximum score of $90$.
Course A has a range of $80$, and Course B has a range of $50$.
Without seeing the minimum scores, which course has the lower minimum score, and what is it?
mastery.solution_text:
Range $=$ maximum $-$ minimum, and both courses share the same maximum of $90$.
Course A: minimum $=90-80=10$.
Course B: minimum $=90-50=40$.
Course A has the lower minimum score, of $10$.
